What generative AI does

It creates a draft from your request and the information available to it.

  • It can help write, summarize, and organize.
  • It can also leave things out or add incorrect details.
Miguel Guhlin03 / 31

Generative AI is software that creates something, such as text or an image, from a request. In this workshop, I will use ChatGPT to work with text and files. Think of the answer as a draft that needs your attention. A useful draft may save us time, but fluent writing does not tell us whether every detail is correct. We need to look at the information we supplied and compare it with the answer. I am going to keep our first example small enough that everyone can do that comparison without opening a complicated packet.

Source: ChatGPT prompting guide

Words for our first chat

A prompt is simply your request.

WordEveryday meaning
ChatbotThe app you talk with, such as ChatGPT
ModelThe AI system the app uses to create an answer
Prompt / inputYour request and the information you give it
Response / outputThe answer or draft you receive
Miguel Guhlin04 / 31

These words describe things you will see as we work. A chatbot is the app where the conversation happens. A model is the AI system the app uses to create an answer. A prompt is your request. Input includes that request and any information you provide, such as a note or an attached file. Output is what comes back. I will usually say request and answer because those words are enough for our exercises. You do not need a special formula. Clear everyday language is a good place to start, and you can follow up when an answer needs changing.

A first request

One small job using a made-up note

Using this note only, write a friendly one-sentence reminder: “Applications close October 1.”
  • No real applicant information is needed.
  • I can check the date and length myself.

Try the first request

Miguel Guhlin05 / 31

I will open a fresh ChatGPT chat and type this request. The note is made up for practice. We want a friendly reminder, one sentence long, and we want the deadline to stay October 1. I will pause before sending so you can see the whole request. After the answer appears, I will read it with you. Did it keep the date? Did it stay within one sentence? Did it add any new rule or promise? If the live tool is unavailable, the practice page has a clearly labeled prepared example we can inspect together.

Useful background information

Context means the information that helps AI do the job.

DetailOur reminder example
Audience: who will read itStudents applying for a scholarship
Tone: how it should soundFriendly and direct
Source: where facts come fromThe supplied deadline note
Limit: what it must avoidNo invented dates, links, or promises
Miguel Guhlin06 / 31

Context means useful background information. For this reminder, the audience is the students who will read it. Tone means how the writing sounds, such as friendly or formal. A source is where the facts come from. A limit tells the tool what it should avoid. You may also see people assign AI a role, such as writing assistant. That can help explain the kind of help wanted, but it does not make the tool a qualified reviewer. I add details when they matter to the result. I do not need a long description of an imaginary expert to write a simple reminder.

A clearer request

The same job with the useful details included

Write a friendly reminder for scholarship applicants. Use only this note: “Applications close October 1.” Write one sentence. Keep the date exactly as written. Do not add links or promises.
  • Job + source + audience + format + limits
Miguel Guhlin07 / 31

This request still does one small job. I have added who the message is for, the information it may use, and the form I want. Format means the shape of the answer. Here that shape is one sentence; later it will be a table. I have also named what must remain unchanged. I will compare this answer with the first one. The longer request is useful only if those added details improve what we need. A short request can work well. We should judge the answer by the task, rather than assume more words always produce a better result.

What a good answer looks like

Evaluation criteria are the checks we choose in advance.

Prepared example: “A friendly reminder: scholarship applications close October 1.”
  • Correct date: October 1
  • Requested format: one sentence
  • No added rules, links, or promises
Miguel Guhlin08 / 31

Evaluation criteria is a formal phrase for the checks we use to judge an answer. In this example, we have only three: keep the date, use one sentence, and avoid adding information. The answer on this slide is a prepared teaching example, not a captured response from a live model. Your actual response may use different wording. That is fine if it passes the checks. I will ask a participant to inspect the date and someone else to look for an added promise. When we later use a scoring guide, we will make those checks just as visible.

Improving a request

A short practice cycle

StepWhat I do
1. Choose the taskName one result I need
2. Write a requestAdd the facts and limits that matter
3. Try and checkCompare the answer with my checks
4. Improve and saveFix a problem; keep the useful request
Miguel Guhlin09 / 31

This practice cycle adapts the four-step prompt builder in my Creating with Generative AI materials, especially pages 24, 38, 39, and 42. First I choose a task. Then I write a request with the information needed for that task. I try it and compare the answer with the checks I chose. If something is wrong or unclear, I change the request and try again. Saving a useful request can save work next time, but I still need to check each new answer. I invite you to name one office task small enough to try this way. A reminder or a short checklist is a good starting point.

Source: Creating with Generative AI — Miguel Guhlin

Source: ChatGPT prompting guide

Examples and follow-up requests

You can show the style you want and ask for a change.

Follow-up: “Make it warmer. Keep one sentence and keep October 1 unchanged.”
  • An example shows the kind of answer I want.
  • A follow-up improves the answer I just received.
  • A sequence of small requests is often called prompt chaining.
Miguel Guhlin10 / 31

You can talk to the tool again after the first answer. This follow-up asks for a warmer tone while preserving the date and length. An example can also help: I might show one reminder in the style I like and ask for another with the supplied facts. You may hear zero-shot for no example, one-shot for one example, and few-shot for a few examples. Those names are optional vocabulary. The useful idea is showing what you mean. Prompt chaining means dividing work into connected requests. We can draft a reminder, check its facts, and then adjust its tone.

Source: ChatGPT prompting guide

AI can add a false detail

A confident answer still needs a fact check.

  • Original: “I ran 12 tutoring sessions.”
  • AI added: “Grades improved by 20%.”
  • The original does not support the added claim.
Miguel Guhlin11 / 31

This picture shows a mistake we can check without special expertise. The original says the applicant ran twelve tutoring sessions. The AI draft adds an improvement in grades, but the original never says that. I would remove the extra claim and check the rest of the answer. People sometimes call an invented AI detail a hallucination. My earlier deck uses that term on page 59. The practical response is to compare it with the original information. Asking AI to say how confident it feels does not supply the missing evidence. Asking it to review its own answer can help find problems, but a person still needs to check the facts.

Source: Creating with Generative AI — Miguel Guhlin

Files in the practice packet

File endings tell us what kind of file we are opening.

EndingWhat it means here
.csvA simple table, such as the application records
.mdPlain text with simple headings; called Markdown
.txtPlain text, such as a saved prompt
.pdfA document with a fixed page layout
Miguel Guhlin12 / 31

The practice packet is a folder of small files you can open and inspect. CSV holds a simple table, with one row per record. Markdown, usually ending in dot md, is ordinary text with simple marks for headings or lists. TXT is plain text. A PDF preserves a document’s page layout. This builds on the file examples on pages 27 to 30 of my earlier deck. There is no single file type that guarantees AI will read everything correctly. If a file cannot be read, stop that part of the task and say what is missing. In our packet, the listed pretend PDFs are not included; the actual exercise uses the small text and CSV files.

A person owns the decision

AI can prepare a checklist. Staff check it and decide.

  • Use the AI account and information your organization allows.
  • Names removed from a file do not remove every identifying detail.
  • Practice here uses made-up information.
Miguel Guhlin13 / 31

Before I supply real applicant information, I need to know which account, tool, and task my organization allows. Removing names is not enough, because stories, schools, or other details may identify a person. I will use made-up information for every demonstration today. AI can help prepare a list of questions or point out a late date. A staff member checks the actual records and applies the organization’s rules. Staff also own final scores and award decisions. The picture shows the relationship I want: the computer supplies a checklist, and the person checks it before making a decision.

Applicant codes in our examples

A17, A18, and A19 are made-up labels used instead of names.

  • The same code connects one applicant’s records.
  • A17-transcript.pdf means the transcript file for applicant A17.
  • A code alone does not make real information anonymous.
Miguel Guhlin14 / 31

I want to explain these labels before we use the packet. A17 is a made-up applicant code, not a person you are expected to recognize. A18 and A19 represent two other made-up applicants. The same code appears across the files so we can connect each person’s records without using a name. For example, A17-transcript dot pdf means the transcript file associated with applicant A17. Using a code can reduce direct identification, but it does not remove every identifying detail in a real application. Our workshop files contain made-up information, so no actual applicant is involved.

NSPA 2026 · Scholarship review practice

A manifest is a file list

A listed file name tells us what to look for.

  • manifest.csv lists pretend document names.
  • The pretend PDFs are not included.
  • A person must open an actual document to check its contents.
Miguel Guhlin15 / 31

Manifest is another word that can sound more complicated than it is. Here it means a file list. Our manifest lists pretend filenames for each applicant. Seeing A17-transcript dot pdf on the list tells us that the name appears there. It does not tell us what grades are in that transcript or whether the transcript meets a requirement. In fact, those pretend PDFs are not included. We are practicing how to organize a list and identify questions for staff. I will stop any answer that claims to have read one of those unavailable documents.

NSPA 2026 · Scholarship review practice

Words in a scoring guide

A rubric describes how to award points.

WordWhat it means
CriterionThe part we are judging, such as community contribution
AnchorThe description of what earns a particular score
EvidenceThe original words or facts supporting a score
Provisional scoreA suggested score for a person to check
Miguel Guhlin16 / 31

A rubric is a scoring guide. A criterion is one part of that guide, such as community contribution. An anchor describes the evidence needed for a particular score. Evidence is the original information supporting the judgment, and we need to know where to find it. A provisional score is a suggestion that a person must check; it is not a final decision. I will use these words on the practice page because they appear in the saved prompts. When we reach the scoring exercise, I will show the whole guide so nobody needs to guess what the scores mean.

A19 is the applicant code for this made-up case.

Original recordWhat it tells us
Recorded date: October 2After the October 1 deadline
Extra time requestedStaff need to review the request

The community contribution scoring guide

Each anchor describes what earns that score.

AnchorCommunity contribution evidence
0No relevant activity described
1Activity named, but applicant role unclear
2Specific applicant contribution
3Specific contribution and a supported result
Miguel Guhlin23 / 31

Here is the complete made-up scoring guide for the third demonstration. Zero means the statement describes no relevant activity. One means an activity appears, but the applicant’s role is unclear. Two means the applicant describes a specific contribution. Three requires that contribution and a supported result. The guide judges contribution, so polished language alone does not earn extra points. I will read these descriptions aloud before asking for any score. We need the actual descriptions available to the model, and a human reviewer must check the suggested match against both the guide and the original statement.

A suggested score needs a quote and a reason.

Compare A17 and A18 with the community contribution guide. Quote the original words, suggest a score, and explain what information is missing. A person checks the score.
  • Files: statements.md and rubric.md
  • Source location = where to find the original words

Open and copy the full scoring prompt

Miguel Guhlin24 / 31

I will supply the statements and the complete rubric, then copy the full prompt from the practice page. We are comparing A17 and A18, which are our made-up applicant codes. I want the original quotation, its section, the suggested score, and an explanation using the guide. I also want to know what evidence is missing for the next score. The prompt calls the score provisional, which means a person must check it. We should not infer character or rank the applicants from these excerpts. I will verify each quoted word before discussing the suggested score.

The same work earns the same contribution score

Prepared teaching comparison

CodeStatement summarySuggested score
A1712 tutoring sessions; recruited 2 volunteers2 of 3
A1812 tutoring days; got 2 volunteers to help2 of 3
  • Both describe a specific contribution.
  • Neither excerpt supplies a supported result.
Miguel Guhlin25 / 31

These statements use different wording for equivalent contribution evidence. Both describe twelve tutoring sessions or days and recruiting two volunteers. Under this guide, both support a suggested score of two. Neither excerpt supplies a supported result, so we do not have the evidence needed for three. The comparison is prepared teaching material, and these shortened phrases are summaries; the original wording is in statements dot md. I will compare the actual quotations there. If AI gives different scores, I will ask which fact in the contribution guide explains the difference. Writing polish alone cannot supply a greater contribution.

A ChatGPT Project

A place to keep related chats, files, and instructions together

One chatA Project
Useful for a single taskUseful when related work continues
Supply the task informationKeep shared practice files available
Give instructions for this chatAdd instructions for the Project
  • Optional next step: Scholarship Review Practice
Miguel Guhlin26 / 31

A Project is a way to keep related work together. Instead of providing the same practice files and standing instructions in every new chat, I can put them in a practice Project when the account supports that feature. Each task can still have its own chat. The Project does not guarantee that the answer is correct, and it does not give us permission to upload applicant data. I will use the fictional packet and name the sources needed for each task. If Projects are unavailable, the fresh-chat method we already used remains a useful way to practice.

Instructions for repeated work

Instructions are the rules I want AI to follow.

Use only the supplied practice files. Show the original words and where to find them. Say when information is missing. Leave final decisions to staff.
  • A prompt names today’s task.
  • Project instructions apply to work inside that Project.

Read or copy the complete practice instructions

Miguel Guhlin27 / 31

Instructions are rules for how the work should happen. This short example explains the most important ideas in the complete practice instructions. A prompt tells the tool what I need on this occasion. Project instructions keep relevant rules with the ongoing practice work. Personal custom instructions can express preferences across chats, but private program details should stay with the appropriate task or Project. I will inspect every answer even when instructions are saved. If a source document contains a request to ignore our rules, that is part of the source text to examine, not permission to change the review process.

A skill is a reusable recipe

It saves the steps for a task I expect to repeat.

Recipe partEvidence-review example
IngredientsAn applicant excerpt and the scoring guide
StepsQuote, compare, explain a gap
Check before useTry examples where I know the answer

Explore the reusable evidence-review skill

Miguel Guhlin28 / 31

I think of a skill as a reusable recipe. This builds on the reusable-instruction steps on pages 61, 62, and 70 of my earlier deck. It describes what information is needed, how to carry out the task, and how to check the result. Our evidence-review skill asks for a statement and a scoring guide, then returns quotations, a suggested match, and missing information for a person to check. We can try the written procedure manually in a chat. Tools differ in how they install and run skills, so I do not assume one installation method works everywhere. Before relying on it, I will try known examples, missing information, and a misleading instruction inside a source.

Fair rules for applicant use of AI

Applicants need clear expectations before they apply.

  • State what help is allowed and what must be disclosed.
  • A tool’s “AI-written” flag can be wrong.
  • Staff check concerns and give applicants a fair chance to explain.

Read the policy examples

Miguel Guhlin29 / 31

Our review process also needs clear expectations for applicants. We should publish what kinds of help are allowed and how applicants should disclose that help. If a detection tool flags an essay, the flag does not prove who wrote it or that a rule was broken. An unflagged essay is not proof either. Staff should examine the concern under the published policy, give the applicant a fair chance to explain, and record the decision. The practice page includes sample language for local discussion. Each organization still needs to decide its own rules and how someone can request another review.

Source: Turnitin AI Writing Report guidance

My next small practice task

One request I can check myself

  • Choose one made-up note or practice file.
  • Write the result I want and what must stay accurate.
  • Check the answer against the original.
  • Keep the request and note what I had to fix.

Return to my awareness self-check

Miguel Guhlin30 / 31

I invite you to choose one small task to try after the session. You can use the reminder example, the file-list demonstration, or one statement and the scoring guide. Write down the result you want and what you will check before you send the request. After the answer appears, compare it with the original. Keep a note of anything you changed, including a false detail, a missing item, or an unclear instruction. Then try again with that improvement. You can revisit the self-check and choose one next step. There is no need to master every feature before practicing one useful task.
